nameStory: The 'longbract' part of this spiderwort's name comes from the extra-long, leaf-like bracts (modified leaves) that sit right below its flower clusters, making them much more prominent than in other spiderworts. The 'spiderwort' name comes from the stringy, mucilaginous sap that oozes from broken stems and leaves, creating web-like strands that early settlers thought resembled spider silk.
description: Longbract spiderwort is a clumping perennial wildflower with grass-like leaves and three-petaled purple flowers that bloom in late spring and early summer. The plant grows 1-2 feet tall with long, narrow leaves that arch gracefully from the base. What makes this spiderwort special are the prominently long, leafy bracts that extend well beyond the flower clusters, giving the whole plant a distinctive appearance. It's quite rare in New England, being much more at home on the Great Plains.

idTips.label: Bracts
idTips.description: Look for the unusually long, leaf-like bracts that extend far beyond the flower cluster - they're much longer than in other spiderworts and are the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Three-petaled purple flowers about an inch across that open in the morning and close by afternoon, with prominent yellow stamens that feel fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, grass-like leaves that fold lengthwise and feel smooth but slightly succulent, growing in clumps from the base

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps 1-2 feet tall and wide, with multiple flowering stems arising from the leafy base in late spring

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: When stems or leaves are broken, they ooze a clear, stringy, mucilaginous sap that feels slippery and stretches like spider silk

habitat: In New England, this prairie native is extremely rare and typically found only in sunny, well-drained grasslands or prairie remnants, often on sandy or gravelly soils. Look for it in areas that mimic its native Great Plains habitat - open fields, meadows, or restored prairie plantings where it may have been intentionally introduced.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in early spring as grass-like shoots from the ground, with flower buds beginning to form by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from May through July, with the distinctive long bracts and purple flowers most visible in early morning before the flowers close for the day.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back in fall, with seed capsules splitting open to release small black seeds.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground growth visible, surviving as underground rootstock.

funFact: Each individual flower only lasts for one day, opening in the morning and closing forever by afternoon, but the plant produces new flowers daily for weeks - it's like nature's own daily calendar!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the more common Virginia spiderwort, but longbract spiderwort's bracts extend much farther beyond the flowers - think of them as wearing an extra-long green hat compared to Virginia spiderwort's shorter cap.
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily a Great Plains species that's quite rare in New England - most sightings here are likely garden escapes or intentional prairie plantings rather than truly wild populations. Don't expect to find this casually while hiking!
compareHints: Compared to Virginia spiderwort (the most common spiderwort in New England), longbract spiderwort has much longer bracts extending well beyond the flower clusters, while Ohio spiderwort has hairless leaves (longbract's are slightly hairy). The long bracts are really the dead giveaway - no other spiderwort in our region has bracts quite so prominently extended.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virginia spiderwort is the most common spiderwort in New England and has the classic blue-purple flowers and smooth leaves.
Ohio spiderwort differs from Virginia spiderwort mainly in its hairless sepals and slightly more robust growth habit.
Unlike its native New England spiderwort cousins like Virginia spiderwort, Purple Heart has distinctly purple foliage year-round rather than green leaves.
Unlike our native Virginia spiderwort with its grass-like leaves and blue flowers, inchplant has broad, striped leaves and rarely flowers indoors.
